1.pericope_label: Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world. Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God: And every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God: and this is that spirit of antichrist, whereof ye have heard that it should come; and even now already is it in the world.

schools.summary: Read the opening as a present imperative with the negative and translate accordingly, stop believing, since some had clearly already been carried away by the errors then rampant, Docetic on one side and Cerinthian on the other; add that credulity is only gullibility, and that believers still fall easy victims to the latest fads in spiritualistic humbuggery. Take the verb for trying from the assayer's bench: put them to the acid test as the metallurgist does his metals, so that what stands is approved and what fails is rejected, the two words being Paul's own. Note that the warning is old, given by Jesus himself against false prophets and false Christs working portents, and that the perfect tense means they are abroad always. On the test itself insist that a form of words settles nothing; the point is not that pronouncing the sentence proves a man a Christian but that holding and teaching it marks him an advocate of truth rather than an apostle of error, and the proposed rendering that would make the clause say Jesus who came in the flesh is the Christ should be refused, being neither the obvious sense nor the usual idiom. Secure the confession grammatically by preferring the perfect participle to the infinitive, so that the phrase describes Jesus as already come in real humanity and not in the phantom body the Docetists allowed him. Then handle the Latin reading in which the false teacher dissolves or divides Jesus, trace it through the Fathers and the old copies, and reject it as having no authority in the Greek manuscripts, versions or usage, and as manifestly of Latin origin, probably a marginal gloss that worked its way in against the errors of the day — while granting that it points at a second heresy, the splitting of Jesus from Christ, where the earlier clause meets the first. Note finally that the repeated words about the flesh in the third verse are no part of the text, and that the prophecy of antichrist had found fulfilment before the Church looked for it.

Define the term before anything else: by spirit is meant either every doctrine pretended to come from the Spirit of God or every teacher professing to be qualified and sent by him, and the second is the better sense, so that the whole passage may be paraphrased as distinguishing the teacher of God from the teacher of antichrist. Explain why the subject returns here, since many abused the name of Christ to serve their own errors, some making a half profession and so getting the better opportunity to injure his cause; and observe that Satan takes his occasion through Christ himself, who is the stone of offence against whom all stumble who keep not the way. Then answer the objection that so many errors discredit the gospel: it is perpetual with the gospel that Satan attempts to pollute its purity by variety of errors, and if this age has brought forth horrible and monstrous sects, so that many stand amazed and, not knowing where to turn, cast aside all care for religion, they act most foolishly, for by shunning the light of truth they cast themselves into the darkness. Unfold what the confession contains: that Christ came proves he was before with the Father, and so his eternal divinity; that he came in flesh means he put on our nature and became a real man, our brother, free only from sin and corruption; and the end of his coming must be noticed too. Say what the confessing not covers — the proper deity and sonship, the true humanity, the Messiahship, the offices and ordinances, the satisfaction and righteousness, and the fact that pardon and life are by him. On the last verse, note that the antichristian kingdom was already in the world because it carried on its iniquity in secret, though the truth had not yet been subverted by spurious dogmas, superstition had not yet corrupted worship, the world had not yet perfidiously departed, and tyranny had not yet openly exalted itself.

Say plainly that we must not be forward to believe every teacher a man sent of God, and explain the usage historically: in those early times every teacher professed to be inspired, because all the prophets had come thus accredited, so the word spirit came to stand for the man who claimed to teach under the Spirit's influence. Name the touchstone rather than describe the method — try them by that testimony which is known to have come from the Spirit of God, the word of revelation already given, to the law and to the testimony, and if any man speak not according to these, the spirit that actuates him is not of God. Set out the chapter's course in a sentence or two before beginning, that those who deny Christ come in the flesh have the spirit of antichrist, that the followers of God have been enabled to discern and overcome them, that love to God and one another is shown necessary from God's love to us, and that though no man has seen God every genuine Christian knows him by the Spirit given. On the confession, require it both with heart and voice, and observe that this coming presupposes, contains and draws after it the whole doctrine of Christ, since no man can call Jesus Lord but by the Holy Ghost. Then attend to the text of the third verse: the words about coming in the flesh are wanting in the chief uncials, in the Syriac, Arabic, Ethiopic, Coptic, Armenian and Latin versions, and in Origen, Cyril, Theodoret and Irenaeus, and Griesbach has left them out. Take the spirit of antichrist to cover all the opponents of the incarnation, and so of the passion, death and resurrection and the benefits derived from them, and say that it was working powerfully already among Jews and Gentiles alike.

Divide the apostle's charge into caution and scrutiny. To caution: regard not, trust not, follow not every pretender to the Spirit of God, every professor of vision or inspiration or revelation. To scrutiny: the claims laid to the Spirit are to be examined, and the disciples are allowed a judgment of discretion in reference to the spirits that would be believed and trusted in the affairs of religion. Give the reason from the counterfeits themselves, and take care to reason from them in the right direction: truth is the foundation of simulation, and there had been real communications from the divine Spirit, and it is precisely because of that that others pretended to the same. God will take the way of his own wisdom and goodness though it may be liable to abuse; he has sent inspired teachers to the world and given us a supernatural revelation, and the fact that others are evil and impudent enough to pretend the same does not withdraw the gift, it only makes the trying necessary. Recall that a time came when the spiritual man, the man who made a great noise and boast about the Spirit, was called mad by the prophet. Then account for the crop of false prophets by the circumstances of the age, since there was about the time of the Saviour's appearance a general expectation among the Jews of a Redeemer to Israel, and expectation of that kind breeds impostors.

sides.position: Either a doctrine pretended to come from the Spirit, or a teacher professing to be sent by him
A teacher claiming, rightly or falsely, to be influenced by God's Spirit — the whole passage may be paraphrased so
The man who pretended to teach under the Spirit's influence, since in those early times every teacher professed inspiration as the prophets had
Whereby any teacher is actuated

debates.question: What does the existence of counterfeits prove?

sides.position: That there were real communications, since truth is the foundation of simulation; God will take the way of his own wisdom though it be liable to abuse
That Satan works perpetually to pollute the gospel's purity, so that those who throw over religion because sects amaze them cast themselves into the dark
That the false prophets are abroad always, an old story that recurs again and again

debates.question: Should the Latin reading that has the teacher dissolving Jesus be admitted?

sides.position: No: it has no authority in the Greek manuscripts or versions, is manifestly of Latin origin, and was probably a marginal note that crept in
It is worth noting as an allusion to the heresy that splits Jesus from Christ, where the preceding clause meets the Docetists
The repeated words about coming in the flesh in this verse are themselves no part of the text, and Griesbach has left them out

outliers.note: Alone brings the warning into the present, calling credulity gullibility and observing that believers still fall easy victims to the latest fads in spiritualistic humbuggery.
Alone reasons from the counterfeit back to the genuine, arguing that imitation presupposes something worth imitating and that the pretenders therefore prove real communications had been made.

themes: try the spirits, whether they are of God
every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh
the spirit of antichrist, even now already in the world

4.pericope_label: Ye are of God, little children, and have overcome them: because greater is he that is in you, than he that is in the world. They are of the world: therefore speak they of the world, and the world heareth them. We are of God: he that knoweth God heareth us; he that is not of God heareth not us. Hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error.

schools.summary: Take the perfect tense of the overcoming as the calm confidence of a final victory, and locate the reason for it not in the disciples but in God who abides in them, greater than the prince of this world however powerful he seems. Insist that no part of the victory was their own strength, and draw the pastoral consequence, that in conflicts with sin, temptation and error the Christian should never despair, since he who dwells in the hearts of Christians is incomparably mightier than the ruler of the darkness of this world. Then describe the opposite party by their speech: their talk proceeds from the world and wins a ready hearing, so that the false prophets and the world are in perfect unison, and the hearers are the gay, the rich, the proud, the ambitious and the sensual, who recognise these teachers as guides because the views accord with their own. Turn that into two tests, one outward and one inward. A professedly religious teacher may determine much about himself by knowing what class of people are pleased with him, and any professed Christian may determine much about his evidences of piety by asking what kind of persons desire his friendship and wish him for a companion; out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, and the general turn of a man's conversation shows what spirit is within him. On the last verse, notice that the writer can simply assume his own standing and argue from it as an indisputable truth, as Paul also does, and turn that into a question for the reader: might not, and ought not, all Christians and all Christian ministers so live that the same thing might be assumed of them, their characters for integrity and purity so clear that no one would be disposed to call them in question? Add the qualification, however, that rejection of the truth may also be due to our not speaking the truth in love.

Fix the antecedent first: the them whom they have overcome are the false prophets of the opening verse, and it is usual with this writer to refer to antecedents at some distance. Then explain the tense pastorally. The object was to animate the faithful so that they might resist impostors boldly, and alacrity is weakened when the issue of the contest is doubtful; it might have caused the good to fear that the kingdom of Christ was hardly set up before enemies stood ready to suppress it. So they are told they have conquered, being already beyond danger though in the middle of the contest, because they will surely be conquerors. Extend the promise: whatever contests we have with the world and the flesh, a certain victory follows, and though hard conflicts succeed one another we fight by Christ's power and are furnished with God's weapons, so that by the very fighting and striving we become conquerors. Ground the comfort in election and regeneration, that they are the children of God by adopting grace and cannot become the servants of men, being kept by the power of God unto salvation and enlightened by the Spirit to discern truth from error. Describe the other party as still what they were when they came into the world, under the pollution and dominion of sin, indulging worldly lusts, supposing gain to be godliness and having men's persons in admiration because of advantage. Correct the rendering of the clause about their speech, since the preposition never means concerning; it means according to, as in the saying that by thy words thou shalt be justified, so the sense is that they speak by the world's own views and principles. Finally warn that the claim to be of God is the easiest of boasts, that false prophets make it as loudly, deceiving under the mask of God, and that the faithful must be content with their own fewness, since it is no diminution of the gospel's authority that many reject it.

Put the overcoming in terms of testimony: their witness, proceeding from the Spirit of Christ, has invalidated the witness proceeding from the influence of Satan, for greater is the Holy Spirit which is in them than the spirit which is in the world — the Spirit of Christ within against the spirit of antichrist without. Take those who are of the world as being of the number of those that know not God, so that they speak from the same principle, wisdom and spirit, and, of consequence, the world hears them with approbation. Then supply a rough working test of teaching. The doctrine and the teacher most prized and followed by worldly men, and by the gay, giddy and garish multitude, are not from God: such teaching savours of the flesh, lays on no restraints, prescribes no cross-bearing, and leaves every one in full possession of his heart's lusts and easily besetting sins; and by this, false doctrine and false teachers are easily discerned. On the other side, say that the apostles have the Spirit of God and speak and teach by that Spirit, and that he who has a truly spiritual discernment acknowledges the doctrine to be from God, since it is spiritual and leads from earth to heaven.

Encourage the disciples against the fear and danger of the seducing spirit by three methods. First, assure them of a more divine principle within: they are God's little children, born of God, taught of God, anointed of God, and so secured against infectious and fatal delusions, since God has his chosen who shall not be mortally seduced. Second, give them hope of victory, since they have overcome these deceivers already and there is good ground to hope they will do so still, on two accounts — that there is a strong preserver within them, the Spirit of God dwelling in them being mightier than men or devils, so that it is a great happiness to be under the influence of the Holy Ghost; and that they are not of the same temper as the deceivers. Third, describe that difference of temper exactly. The Spirit of God has framed the mind of the disciples for God and heaven, whereas the spirit prevailing in the deceivers leads them to this world: their heart is addicted to it, they study its pomp and pleasure and interest, and therefore they speak of the world, professing a worldly messiah, projecting a worldly kingdom and dominion, and engrossing its possessions and treasures to themselves — forgetting that the true Redeemer's kingdom is not of this world. Add that it is this worldly design which procures them their following, for the world hears its own.

Set the whole passage in the figure of the wilderness. This world is to all the faithful seeking their own country what the desert was to the people of Israel: they wandered as yet and were seeking their country, but with God for their guide they could not wander astray, since their way was God's bidding. Observe that where they went about during forty years the journey itself is made up of very few stations, and that they were retarded because they were in training, not because they were forsaken. What God promises us is that ineffable sweetness which eye has not seen nor ear heard, neither has it entered into the heart of man; and meanwhile we are exercised by temporal labours and trained by the temptations of this present life. Then give the practical word: if you would not die of thirst in this wilderness, drink charity, for it is the fountain God has been pleased to place here that we faint not in the way, and we shall drink of it more abundantly when we are come to our own land. Bind it to the prayer just heard, since we have made an agreement with God that if we would have him forgive our sins we also should forgive the sins committed against us, and that which forgives is nothing other than charity: take charity from the heart and hatred possesses it, and hatred does not know how to forgive, while where charity is she forgives fearlessly and is not straitened.

debates.question: Why is the victory spoken of as already won?

sides.position: Because eagerness slackens when the issue is doubtful; they are beyond danger though still in the contest, since they will surely conquer
It is the calm confidence of final victory
Because the strength was never theirs; God dwelling in them is mightier than the ruler of this world
Because they are God's chosen, who shall not be mortally seduced

debates.question: What does it mean that they speak of the world?

sides.position: Not of, since the preposition never means concerning; it means according to, so they speak by the world's own principles
Either that their conversation pertains to the things of this world, or that they are wholly influenced by the love of it
Their talk proceeds from the world and wins a ready hearing; the false prophets and the world are in perfect unison

debates.question: Can a teacher be judged by his following?

sides.position: Yes: a teacher may determine much about himself by knowing what class of people are pleased with him
Yes: the doctrine prized by the gay, giddy and garish multitude lays on no restraint and prescribes no cross-bearing
With a caution: rejection of the truth may also be due to our not speaking the truth in love

outliers.note: Alone reads the passage through the wilderness, making the present world the desert and charity the fountain placed in it so that the travellers do not faint before reaching their own land.
Alone disputes the English rendering of the clause about speaking of the world, arguing from usage elsewhere that the preposition means according to.

themes: greater is he that is in you than he that is in the world
they are of the world, and the world heareth them
the spirit of truth and the spirit of error

7.pericope_label: Beloved, let us love one another: for love is of God; and every one that loveth is born of God, and knoweth God. He that loveth not knoweth not God; for God is love. In this was manifested the love of God toward us, because that God sent his only begotten Son into the world, that we might live through him. Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.

schools.summary: State the origin of love in three propositions: all true love has its origin in God; real love shows that we have his Spirit and belong to him; and it assimilates us to God, making us more like him. Then fence the claim, since the verse cannot mean that every one who loves his wife and children, his classmate, his partner in business, his house or his farms is thereby born of God; what is meant is true love to Christians as such, brotherly love. Allow all the same that even human love comes from God, being a reflection of something in the divine nature itself, and note that persistence in loving, both the indicative and the participle standing in the present, is the proof of having been begotten of God. On the great sentence, guard the grammar: the predicate is without the article, so the writer says God is love and not that love is God, the two terms not being interchangeable, as he elsewhere says God is light and God is spirit. Say what the sentence is for: he is not merely benevolent but benevolence itself, and in the darkness of a world of sin, amid the perplexities that embarrass us about the divine administration, faith may rest in this even where it cannot reconcile what it sees. Measure the manifestation in five quantities — the worth of the soul, its exposure to eternal death, the greatness of the gift, the greatness of his sorrows for us, and the blessedness to which he will raise us — and add that whether saved or lost we shall have an ever-expanding view of that love. On the words themselves, insist that the phrase means in us and not among us or to us; mark the change of tense between the perfect used for the permanent mission and the aorist used for the single event; and note that the writer applies the term only-begotten to Jesus alone, since he alone completely reproduces the nature and character of God.

Take the exhortation as a return to the subject the epistle keeps circling, since it is filled with the doctrine of faith and exhortation to love and passes continually from one to the other; and give the immediate occasion, that where worldly men follow and embrace the false teachers, those who are of God should love one another, love their faithful ministers and stand fast in one spirit. Refuse the counterfeit at once: the command is not discharged by loving friends because they love us, since it is mutual love among the faithful that is enjoined, and no one can prove himself a son of God except he love his neighbours, the true knowledge of God necessarily producing love in us. Then handle the sentence that God is love with unusual caution. Many reason refinedly here, and the ancients especially perverted the passage to prove the divinity of the Spirit; but the meaning is simply that as God is the fountain of love this effect flows from him and is diffused wherever the knowledge of him comes, just as he was called light earlier not because his essence was in question but because there is nothing dark in him. He does not speak of the essence of God but shows only what he is found to be by us. Draw two things from it: that the true knowledge of God is the knowledge which regenerates and renews us, and that it must therefore conform us to the image of God — so away with the foolish gloss about unformed faith, since to separate faith from love is to attempt to take heat from the sun. Grant that many other proofs of divine love exist, in creation, in our dominion over the earth, in our preservation and our understanding, all of which admit no cause but gratuitous love; yet call this the principal evidence, surpassing all, so that whenever we look upon Christ he confirms to us that God is love. Add that God loved us before we were born, when our hearts were turned from him, so that the notion that a man is chosen because God foresees him worthy of love cannot stand.

Turn the exhortation into a measure of the man: he that loves most has most of God in him, and he who loves God and his neighbour is a true child of his heavenly Father, made partaker of the divine nature, which his love proves. Then make the great sentence the centre of everything. Observe that although God is called holy, just and righteous, he is never called holiness or justice in the abstract as he is here called Love; that this seems to be the essence of the divine nature and all other attributes only modifications of it; and that it is his darling and reigning attribute, which sheds an amiable glory upon all his other perfections. Say what it brought the writer, more sweetness even in the hour of writing it than the whole world can bring. Then press the consequences hard: he is an infinite fountain of benevolence to every human being, he hates nothing that he has made and cannot hate because he is love, he causes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, he has made no human being for perdition and has never rendered it impossible by any necessitating decree for a fallen soul to find mercy, and he has given the fullest proof of love to the whole race in the incarnation of his Son, who tasted death for every man. Then ask the question the text seems to force: how can a decree of absolute and unconditional reprobation, of the greater part or of any part of the human race, stand in the presence of such a text as this? On the sending, say that the mission of Christ was the fullest proof God could give or man receive of infinite love to the world; that the whole world was sentenced to death and every individual dead in trespasses; and that it was God's love and not our merit which induced him to devise means that his banished should not be expelled from him.

Press the exhortation by argument rather than assertion, and take the arguments in order. First, from the high and heavenly descent of love: God is the fountain, the author, the parent and the commander of it, and it is the sum of his law and gospel; every one who loves, whose spirit is framed to judicious and holy love, is born of God, since the Spirit of God is the Spirit of love, the new nature in the children of God is the offspring of his love and its very temper and complexion is love, the fruit of the Spirit being love. Love comes down from heaven. Second, from what love argues about the one who has it: he that loves knows God, and he that loves not knows not God, for what attribute of the divine Majesty shines so clearly in all the world as his communicative goodness, which is love? The wisdom, the greatness, the harmony and the usefulness of the vast creation, which so fully demonstrate that he is, demonstrate also what he is; so that a man who has no love has failed to apprehend the plainest thing about the God whose existence he grants.

debates.question: Does the sentence that God is love describe his essence?

sides.position: It is the essence of the divine nature, all other attributes being only modifications of it
It is his darling and reigning attribute, and he is never styled holiness or righteousness in the abstract as he is styled love
No: it does not speak of the essence of God but only shows what he is found to be by us, and the ancients perverted the passage
He is not merely benevolent but benevolence itself
The predicate has no article: God is love, but love is not God, and the terms are not interchangeable

debates.question: How far does love prove regeneration?

sides.position: Every one that loveth is born of God — but not every one who loves his wife, his partner in business or his farms
Even human love comes from God, a reflection of something in the divine nature itself
Not the love that returns what friends have given, which is self-love; but the true knowledge of God necessarily produces love
He that loveth most has most of God in him

debates.question: Is God's love here general or particular?

sides.position: Not his general love to all creatures but his special love toward the elect, secret from everlasting
Free and gratuitous, given before we were born and when our hearts were turned from him, so that election cannot rest on foreseen worthiness
Love toward the whole human race, proved by the incarnation of a Son who tasted death for every man

outliers.note: Alone turns the sentence that God is love into an argument against unconditional reprobation, asking how such a decree can stand in the presence of the text.

Alone denies that the sentence describes God's essence at all, complaining that the ancients perverted it to prove the divinity of the Spirit and insisting it shows only what God is found to be by us.

themes: love is of God, and every one that loveth is born of God
he sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins

11.pericope_label: Beloved, if God so loved us, we ought also to love one another. No man hath seen God at any time. If we love one another, God dwelleth in us, and his love is perfected in us. Hereby know we that we dwell in him, and he in us, because he hath given us of his Spirit. And we have seen and do testify that the Father sent the Son to be the Saviour of the world.

schools.summary: Note the force of the little word so, which emphasises the manifestation of God's love both in its manner and in its extent, and the present tense of the obligation, to keep on loving. Then set the invisibility beside the Gospel's opening, where almost the same words stand with a different verb, and give the sense of the conditional, if we keep on loving one another, God abides in us — else we cannot go on loving one another at all, so that mutual love is a sign of the indwelling of God in men. On the perfecting, enter a caution: it is not that we are absolutely perfect, nor even that our love is perfect, but that love to others is the proper carrying out of love toward him, our love for each other being the exponent of the love that reigns in the heart. Take the giving of the Spirit as the second evidence and mark its tense, the perfect standing where an aorist stood earlier, so that the gift itself is the proof of fellowship; and point to what the Spirit produces, the love, joy, peace, long-suffering, gentleness, goodness and faith of the familiar list, which is among the clearest evidences a man can have that he is a child of God. Then the testimony. Explain why the writer turns to it here: struck with the greatness of the subject, his mind reverts to the evidence on which the whole rests, that he had actually seen the one who was sent. Note that he is qualified to bear witness as the disciples were charged to be, that the perfect of beholding is used again, and that the title Saviour of the world occurs elsewhere in these writings only in the confession of the Samaritans, though the idea is in the Gospel's third chapter.

Begin by observing that the writer uses his master's own language, and that the love in question is what was shown in sending the Son to be a propitiation. Refuse the mercenary version of the duty: our love ought not to be mercenary, for when we regard our own advantage or return good offices to friends it is self-love and not love of others, and we are to love our neighbours as God has loved us, remembering that we have been loved freely. On the invisibility, argue from it toward the brethren: God is invisible in his nature and incomprehensible in his being, so there is no coming to him and conversing with him in a familiar way as one friend converses with another and finds his love increased by sight and conversation; therefore we ought to love the saints, who are visible and may be seen and come at. Distinguish this use from the Gospel's, where the same words were used to say only that God cannot be known except as he has revealed himself in Christ, whereas here the truth is extended, the power of God being comprehended by faith and love so that we know we are his children and that he dwells in us. Then close the circle: God shows himself present when by his Spirit he forms our hearts to brotherly love, and since love is the effect and fruit of the Spirit we cannot truly and sincerely love the brethren unless the Spirit puts forth his power, so that by love we prove that God abides in us, and whoever boasts of having God while not loving the brethren has his falsehood proved by that very want. On the seeing of the last verse, deny that any sort of seeing is meant: it is the seeing which belongs to faith, by which they recognised the glory of God in Christ, and this knowledge flows from the illumination of the Spirit.

Draw the corollary from being loved without desert: we ought to love one another in like manner, and not suspend our love to a fellow-creature either on his moral worth or on his love to us; we should love one another for God's sake, and then no unkind carriage of a brother will induce us to withdraw our love from him, for if it have God for its motive and model it will never fail. On the invisibility, note that the very words stand in the Gospel with one verb changed, and then supply the short answer: we may feel him, though we cannot see him. Take the perfecting as accomplishment, that his love has then its full effect and full accomplishment, having moulded us according to its own nature; and note that the two things named in these verses, the indwelling proved by love and the love perfected, are each taken up and treated at length in what follows. On the testimony, say that Jesus Christ was manifested in the flesh and that the witnesses testify in consequence of the fullest conviction, having had the fullest proof from his doctrine and miracles which they heard and saw during the whole time he sojourned among men; and make the two things named here, the communion of the Spirit and the confession of the Son, the foundation and criteria of our abiding in God and God in us.

Take the article of faith as the foundation of the love commanded, since faith in Christ works love to God and love to God kindles love to the brethren. Then proclaim that article in five heads. The Lord Jesus's relation to God: he is Son to the Father, such a Son as no one else is, and so as to be God with the Father. His relation and office towards us: the Saviour of the world, who saves us by his death, example, intercession, Spirit and power against the enemies of our salvation. The ground on which he became so: the mission of him, the Father decreeing and willing his coming, in and with the consent of the Son. The apostle's assurance of it: he and his brethren had seen the Son of God in his human nature, in his holy converse and works, in his transfiguration on the mount, in his death, his resurrection and his royal ascent to heaven, and had so seen him as to be satisfied that he was the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. And the attestation that follows from such evidence: we have seen, and do testify.

Meet the difficulty of a command so large that no one could be always fulfilling it in words. Love is a sweet word, but sweeter the deed; to be always speaking of it is not in our power, for we have many things to do and divers businesses draw us different ways, so that the tongue has not leisure to be always speaking of love, though indeed it could have nothing better to do. But though we may not always be speaking of it, we may always keep it. Illustrate from the Alleluia being sung at that season: we do not sing it for a whole hour, but barely during a few moments of one, and then give ourselves to something else; and Alleluia means Praise ye the Lord. He that praises God with his tongue cannot be always doing it, but he that praises God by his life and conduct can be doing it always. Works of mercy, affections of charity, sanctity of piety, incorruptness of chastity, modesty of sobriety — these are always to be practised, whether we are in public or at home, before men or in our chamber, speaking or holding our peace, occupied upon something or free from occupation; and they are always to be kept because all these virtues are within.

Establish first that to look upon God with eyes of flesh is impossible, since the incorporeal cannot be subject to bodily sight, and the Only-begotten Son of God has himself testified that no man has seen God at any time. Meet the objection from the prophet who is said to have seen: what the Scripture says is that he saw the likeness of the glory of the Lord, not the Lord himself, and the likeness of the glory, not the glory itself as it really is; and when he saw merely the likeness he fell to the earth from fear. Argue from the lesser to the greater: if the sight of the likeness of the glory brought fear and distress upon the prophets, anyone who should attempt to behold God himself would to a certainty lose his life, according to the saying that no man shall see my face and live. Then turn the invisibility into an act of mercy rather than a defect: for this cause God of his great loving-kindness spread out the heaven as a veil of his proper Godhead, that we should not perish; and say the word is not yours but the prophet's, who asks that God would rend the heavens and come down.

debates.question: What kind of seeing did the witnesses do?

sides.position: Bodily: they saw the works and miracles, the dying and rising and going up
They saw him in his human nature, his works, his transfiguration, his death, resurrection and ascent
Not any sort of seeing, but the seeing that belongs to faith, flowing from the illumination of the Spirit
The perfect of beholding, the same verb as in the earlier verse; he is qualified to bear witness

debates.question: What follows from God being invisible?

sides.position: That anyone attempting to behold him would lose his life, and that heaven was spread as a veil in mercy
That we should love the visible saints instead, since love is not increased by sight and conversation with God
That we cannot become acquainted with him by sight, but we may by love
That we may feel him though we cannot see him

debates.question: In what sense is love perfected in us?

sides.position: Not that we are perfect, nor our love, but that loving others carries out our love toward him
It has its full accomplishment, having moulded us according to its own nature
Mutual love is the sign of the indwelling of God in men

outliers.note: Alone treats the invisibility as a mercy rather than a limitation, holding that heaven was spread out as a veil over the Godhead so that those who looked should not perish.
Alone refuses to let the apostolic seeing be ocular, making it the seeing that belongs to faith and flows from the illumination of the Spirit.

themes: no man hath seen God at any time
if we love one another, God dwelleth in us
the Father sent the Son to be the Saviour of the world

15.pericope_label: Whosoever shall confess that Jesus is the Son of God, God dwelleth in him, and he in God. And we have known and believed the love that God hath to us. God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him. Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world. There is no fear in love; but perfect love casteth out fear: because fear hath torment. He that feareth is not made perfect in love.

schools.summary: Insist that the confession is not lip service: whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God does so in the true sense and from the heart, and the sentence cannot mean that a form of words insincerely spoken proves anything, since the confession of the deity of Christ implies surrender and obedience too. Mark the order in the next verse, that knowing by experience and trusting confidently come before confessing, and that the order stands reversed from the Gospel's; note that believers are the sphere in which the love of God operates. Then handle the disputed phrase about love being made perfect. The margin accords with the Greek in reading love with us, and the phrase should be construed with the verb, standing in contrast to the earlier in us and emphasising cooperation, so that God works with man; or take it of the love that is within us, rendered complete in the manner specified and so preparing us to appear with confidence before the judgment-seat. Say what the boldness is worth: he who has true love to God has nothing to fear at that day and may approach the awful tribunal, where he is to receive the sentence determining his everlasting destiny, without alarm. Explain the ground given for it, that we have the same traits of character which the Saviour had and, resembling him, need not be alarmed at the prospect of meeting him. On the fear, distinguish the kinds: this dread is the dread of a bond-slave, not the reverence of a son nor the obedience owed a father, and it is the exact opposite of boldness. Note that the word for its torment carries the idea of discipline as well as of penalty, unlike the word that means penalty only. Say that perfect love harbours no suspicion and no dread, that it drives fear out of doors by a powerful metaphor, and set out the four conditions of men that have been distinguished — without fear and without love; with fear and without love; with fear and with love; without fear and with love.

Take the confession as the sum of faith, since there is nothing necessary for salvation which faith does not find in Christ, and acknowledge none as confessing but those who truly and from the heart believe, however wisely hypocrites may boast. Guard the same point from the other side by producing the counter-instances: the devils believed and owned that Jesus was the Son of God, and unregenerate men have owned it too, as the centurion did at the cross, who knew nothing of communion with God; so the confession meant here is one attended with believing from the heart unto righteousness and with cheerful obedience from a principle of love. On the next verse, define faith by it: to know and believe is to know by believing, for such knowledge is not attained but by faith, and we hence learn how different an uncertain or doubtful opinion is from faith. Lay out the reasoning in order, that faith in Christ makes God dwell in men, that God is love, and that therefore no one dwells in him except he love his brethren, so that love must reign in us since God unites himself to us. On the perfecting, weigh the versions that read it of God's love with us, and decide against them: it is best understood of our love to God, which is shown genuine by our love to the brethren, since the love of God to us does not admit of degrees, nor does its reality depend upon our love to the saints. Then state the natural case about the judgment before stating the remedy. By nature we dread the presence of God, and justly, for as he is the Judge of the world and our sins hold us guilty, death and hell must come to mind whenever we think of him; hence the dread that makes men shun God as much as they can. But refuse the usual account of the fear that is cast out. Many explain it by setting servile fear against voluntary reverence, and that doctrine is true in itself, but it has nothing in common with this passage, where the teaching is that the love of God seen and known by faith gives a peaceful calm beyond the reach of fear; regard what the Apostle means, not what others think.

Say why so much stress is laid on this confession, the false teachers having denied the reality of the incarnation, and add that the confession implies such a belief in Christ as puts a man in possession of pardoning mercy and the indwelling Spirit; require that it be made openly, in the face of all opposition and danger, and from a principle of loving faith. Describe the perfecting concretely: love is made perfect when God dwells in us and we in him, when the carnal mind that was enmity against him has been cast out and the whole heart filled with the spirit of love and purity, so that love has all its degrees and is all in all, in every power and passion and faculty of the soul. Take the boldness as freedom of speech and liberty of access, since we see in the person of our Judge the one who died for us and regenerated our hearts; and say that no man can contemplate that day with comfort on any other ground than that the blood of Christ has cleansed him and that he is kept by the power of God through faith. Then set out the stages of men in respect of fear and love: a natural man has neither fear nor love; one that is awakened has fear without love; a babe in Christ has love and fear; a father in Christ has love without fear. Describe the man in the middle exactly — he is still uncertain concerning his interest in Christ, and though he has many heavenly drawings and often sits with Christ some moments on a throne of love, he yet feels, from the evils of his heart, a dread of the day of judgment, and is not made perfect in love, not having received the abiding witness that he is begotten of God.

Recommend love to God as love to the first and chief of all amiable beings, who has the confluence of all beauty and excellence in himself and confers on every other being whatever renders it good and amiable. Then recommend it by what it secures at the time when it will be most needed. There must be a day of universal judgment; happy they who shall have holy and confiding boldness before the Judge at that day, who shall be able to lift up their heads and look him in the face, as knowing that he is their friend and advocate; happy they who have such boldness and assurance in the prospect of that day, who look and wait for it and for the Judge's appearing. So do, and so may do, the lovers of God, for their love to God assures them of God's love to them, and consequently of the friendship of the Son of God who is to be their judge.

Open by reminding the hearers what remains to be expounded and by making the debt itself an example of the thing commended. This charity, which in this epistle is chiefly and almost alone commended, at once makes us most faithful in paying our debts and you most sweet in exacting your rights. Say most sweet in exacting deliberately, because where charity is not, he that exacts is bitter; but where charity is, both he that exacts is sweet and he of whom it is exacted finds that though he undertakes some labour, charity makes the very labour to be almost no labour, and light. Then prove it from the animals, where the love is not spiritual but carnal and natural. The mother yields herself with great affection to her young when they will have the milk which is their right, and however impetuously the suckling rushes at the teats, that is better for the mother than that it should not suck nor exact what love owes it. We often see great calves driving their heads at the udders with a force that almost lifts the mother's body, yet she does not kick them off; and if the young one is not there to suck, the lowing of the dam calls for it to come.

Apply the verse where the message of the angel divides one company from another. After the vision of the angels Jesus came as his own herald, and the Gospel says that he met them saying All hail, and that they came and took hold of his feet — they took hold of him, that it might be fulfilled, I will hold him and will not let him go. Praise the women for it: though weak in body her spirit was manful, and many waters quench not love, neither do rivers drown it, for he was dead whom they sought and yet the hope of the resurrection was not quenched in them. Then mark the discrimination in the angel's word. He says fear not ye; he does not say to the soldiers, fear not, but to these. As for the soldiers, let them be afraid, that taught by experience they may bear witness and say, Truly this was the Son of God; but you ought not to be afraid, for perfect love casteth out fear. And when the Gospel says that they departed with joy yet full of fear, do not treat it as a contradiction, for the psalm which relates the passion says, Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice.

sides.position: Ours to God, not God's to us, since God's love admits no degrees and does not depend on ours
God's love to us, poured out so abundantly that it appears complete
The love that is within us, rendered complete in the manner specified
The phrase goes with the verb and marks cooperation, so that God works with man
Not the filial fear that is the beginning of wisdom, but the fear of men or the dread of judgment
The dread of a bond-slave, the opposite of boldness, whose torment carries discipline as well as penalty
Slavish fear; a natural man has neither fear nor love, the awakened fear without love, a babe both, a father love without fear
Not servile fear as against filial reverence at all — that distinction, true in itself, has nothing to do with this passage, which contrasts torment with calm

debates.question: What secures boldness at the judgment?

sides.position: Having the same traits of character the Saviour had, so that we need not be alarmed at meeting him
Seeing in the person of our Judge the one who died for us; no man can contemplate that day with comfort on any other ground
Love to God, which assures us of God's love and so of the friendship of the Judge
Charity, which makes even the exacting of a debt sweet and the labour light

outliers.note: Alone rejects the servile-and-filial distinction as foreign to the passage, granting the doctrine true in itself but insisting the contrast here is between torment and calm, and adding that he regards what the apostle means rather than what others think.

Alone illustrates the sweetness charity gives to exacting a debt from the dumb animals, where the cow does not kick off the calves that drive their heads at her udder, and calls for the young one when it is absent.

themes: he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God
boldness in the day of judgment

19.pericope_label: We love him, because he first loved us. If a man say, I love God, and hateth his brother, he is a liar: for he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen, how can he love God whom he hath not seen? And this commandment have we from him, That he who loveth God love his brother also.

schools.summary: Note first that the verb has the same form for statement and for exhortation and take it as a statement, God having loved us before we loved him, our love being a response to his; note too that no object is expressed. Then raise the harder question of what the clause asserts. It admits two explanations: that the fact of his loving first is the ground or reason why we love him, or that we have as a matter of fact been brought to love him in consequence of the love he has shown, while the real ground of our love is the excellence of his own character. If the first were the only ground, the love would be mere selfishness, and it cannot be believed that this was meant; benefits received are indeed a proper reason for love, and we are bound to love God in proportion to what we have received from his hand, but genuine love to God cannot be explained by that alone. There is that in the divine nature which a holy being will love apart from the benefits he is to receive and from any thought of his own destiny. On the argument from the seen to the unseen, take it as an appeal to human nature as it is, since it is more reasonable to expect that we should love one whom we have seen and known personally, and every one feels that we are more likely to love a familiar person than a stranger. Soften the charge of lying, since it is not necessary to suppose deliberate deceit, only that the profession must be false. Note that the verb for seeing is the form used of seeing God in the Gospel's first chapter, and that the negatives are all present, a man who does not keep on loving not being able to keep on loving God. Finally make the command bind as hard as the first: if one is obeyed the other ought to be, and a man can have no evidence that he is a true Christian unless he shows love to his brethren as well as to God.

Guard the priority of God's love so that nothing may be ascribed to ours. His love is prior, from everlasting as well as to everlasting; the choosing in Christ, the blessing with all spiritual blessings, the covenant of grace made from eternity, the gift of grace before the world began and the promise of eternal life all show its antiquity, and his love in regeneration and conversion is previous to ours and the cause of it, since grace brings faith and love with it and produces them in the heart. On the form of the verb, allow that it may be indicative or imperative and prefer the indicative, since the writer is repeating what he has just said, that as God anticipated us by his free love we ought to return love to him — and he immediately infers that God must be loved in men; if the imperative be preferred the sense is nearly the same. Then face the weakness of the argument that follows honestly. It reasons from the lesser to the greater, and there are two obvious exceptions: the love we have to God is from faith and does not flow from sight, and the love of God is far different from the love of men, since God draws his people by his infinite goodness while men are often worthy of hatred. Answer that the Apostle takes as granted what ought to be evident, that God offers himself to us in men who bear his image, and requires the duties he does not need himself to be performed to them, as the psalm says that my goodness reaches not to thee, O Lord, but toward the saints who are on the earth is my love. Add that a shared nature, the need of so many things and mutual intercourse must allure us to mutual love unless we are harder than iron. Say also that the profession and the hatred agree no better than black with white or hot with cold; and take the closing command as the strongest argument of all, drawn from the authority and doctrine of Christ, so that we must so begin with God that a transition is at the same time made to men.

Lay out three grounds of our love to God without ranking them: we love him because we find that he has loved us; we love him from a sense of obligation and gratitude; and we love him from the influence of his own love, shed abroad in our hearts, which is the seed whence our love springs. Report that two of the old versions render the clause as an exhortation, let us therefore love him because he first loved us. Call the sentence the sum of all religion and the genuine model of Christianity, and ask why, since none can say more, any one should say less or say it less intelligibly. Then give the passage a historical target, since much of this epistle seems levelled against those who professed great love to God while hating the nations outside, a leaven which some who came into the Christian Church brought with them, and it required a vision to redeem even Peter's mind from that principle. Distinguish the two ways love toward a brother is excited: by a consideration of his excellences and amiable qualities, which draws a love of complacency and delight, and by a view of his miseries and distresses, which draws a love of compassion and pity; and note that the brother is one daily presented to the senses, to raise esteem and move kindness. Then draw the conclusion the epistle is driving at. The love of God and the love of man can never be separated, and the brother is to be loved whoever he is, whatever his opinions or his mode of worship, purely because he is the child and bears the image of God. Bigotry is properly the want of this pure and universal love: a bigot loves only those who embrace his opinions and receive his way of worship, and he loves them for that, and not for Christ's sake.

debates.question: Is the first clause a statement or an exhortation?

sides.position: A statement; the form is indicative, and no object is expressed
It may be either, but the statement is more suitable, and the sense is nearly the same on both
Two of the old versions render it let us therefore love him

debates.question: Is being loved first the ground of our love?

sides.position: It is a proper reason, but not the original ground, which is the excellence of the divine character apart from any benefit; otherwise the love would be mere selfishness
Three grounds together: that he has loved us, obligation and gratitude, and his love shed abroad as the seed ours springs from
His love is prior in election, covenant and regeneration, and is the cause of ours
This is the sum of all religion; none can say more, so why should any say less

debates.question: Is the argument from the seen to the unseen sound?

sides.position: Yes, as an appeal to human nature: we are likelier to love the familiar than the stranger
It looks weak, reasoning from lesser to greater, since our love to God is from faith and not sight, and men are often worthy of hatred; but God offers himself in those who bear his image
The contradiction is plain enough: profession and hatred agree no better than black with white

outliers.note: Alone names bigotry as the precise failure the commandment addresses, defining it as loving only those who hold one's opinions and keep one's way of worship, and loving them for that and not for Christ's sake.

Alone warns that if being loved first were the only ground of loving God the love would be mere selfishness, and locates the true ground in the excellence of the divine character apart from any benefit.

themes: we love him, because he first loved us
he that loveth not his brother whom he hath seen
that he who loveth God love his brother also
